## Abstract
Aims

To investigate the role of chronic low-grade systemic inflammation—specifically high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP)—in mediating the relationship between ageing and vascular dysfunction, and to assess its causal contribution relative to lipid metabolism. We also examined sex-specific mediation to evaluate differences in inflammatory pathways between men and women.

…

We analysed data from the Rotterdam Study, including 7591 participants with longitudinal carotid intima-media thickness (cIMT) and 6488 with cross-sectional pulse wave velocity (PWV) data. Mediation analysis assessed the roles of hsCRP, total cholesterol, and high-density lipoprotein in the age–vascular dysfunction association accompanied by sex-stratification.
Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) was conducted to explore the potential causal effects of hsCRP on vascular outcomes. hsCRP significantly mediated the effect of age on cIMT (2.66%, *P* = 0.001) and PWV (2.56%, *P* = 4.95 × 10^−9^), with mediation magnitudes comparable to those of lipid markers and stronger in men compared to women. MR analyses provided genetic support for a potential causal relationship between hsCRP and PWV, but not cIMT.
Conclusion

Systemic inflammation indexed by hsCRP appears to mediate and potentially contribute causally to age-related vascular stiffness, particularly in men. These findings support the role of inflammation in functional vascular ageing and suggest that anti-inflammatory strategies may complement lipid-lowering approaches in reducing cardiovascular risk.

## IntroductioneiCardiovascular diseases (CVD) remain the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and advancing age is among their strongest risk factors. As individuals age, arteries undergo functional and structural changes, including stiffening of the vessel wall and thickening of the intima-media layer.^1^ These vascular ageing processes increase the risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes, yet the underlying biological mechanisms remain incompletely understood.

…

Inflammaging is driven by an imbalance in reactive oxygen species, which leads to oxidative stress and upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-1 (IL-1) and interleukin-6 (IL-6), ultimately increasing levels of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) as a downstream marker and well-established proxy for chronic inflammation.
^7–12^ While inflammation has been linked to vascular dysfunction and remodelling with ageing, findings remain inconsistent across populations.^13–15^ Most observational studies reporting positive associations focus on individuals over the age of 50, raising the question of whether these associations reflect the true onset of inflammaging or simply capture its later consequences.
Even prospective studies are limited in their ability to disentangle these effects due to the gradual accumulation of inflammation over time and the lack of repeated inflammatory measurements. Another important consideration is the potential for sex-specific differences in vascular dysfunction and its determinants. Prior studies suggest that hormonal shifts during menopause may modulate vascular responses in women, whereas men may be more susceptible to pro-inflammatory pathways. Understanding these differences may help uncover divergent mechanisms underlying vascular dysfunction.^16–19^
In this study, we used data from the large, population-based Rotterdam Study (RS) to investigate whether systemic inflammation, as measured by hsCRP, mediates the association between age and subclinical vascular dysfunction. We focused on two key vascular outcomes: pulse wave velocity (PWV) as assessed cross-sectionally and reflecting arterial stiffness^20^ and carotid intima-media thickness (cIMT) assessed longitudinally, reflecting structural arterial remodelling.
^20^ We compared the mediating effects of hsCRP with those of lipid markers (as well-known reference points)—and further employed Mendelian randomization (MR) to assess potential causal relationships. In exploratory analyses, we evaluated sex-stratified mediation effects to explore potential differences in the role of inflammation across sexes.

## Methodse ### Study populations The RS is a prospective, population-based cohort study investigating the incidence and progression of risk factors for chronic diseases in middle-aged and elderly individuals. A full description of the study is available elsewhere,^21–23^ but in brief, RS consists of four sub-cohorts. The first sub-cohort, RS-I, began in 1990 with 7983 participants aged 55 and older from the Ommoord district in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.
In 2000, the cohort expanded to include 3011 participants who had turned 55 or had moved into the area (RS-II). In 2006, it expanded again with 3932 participants aged 45 and older (RS-III). In 2016, the most recent extension of the cohort was established with 3005 persons (RS-IV).
Participants were initially invited to complete a health questionnaire at home for partial data collection, followed by an in-person visit to a dedicated research centre where they underwent clinical examinations, blood sampling, and imaging procedures. Outcome data on morbidity and mortality were continuously collected through linkage with digital files from general practitioners in the study area. The RS complies with the Declaration of Helsinki and has been approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of the Erasmus MC (registration number MEC 02.1015) and by the Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (Population Screening Act WBO, licence number 1071272-159521-PG).

…

For this study, we included participants from the first three sub-cohorts (RS-I, RS-II, and RS-III) who had available baseline data on age, inflammation, lipids, and at least one vascular outcome (*n* = 14 926). Participants without follow-up cIMT measurements were excluded (*n* = 7335), resulting in 7591 participants for the longitudinal cIMT mediation analysis.
For the PWV mediation analysis, we included 6488 participants with available cross-sectional PWV data. Longitudinal data on PWV are not yet available in the RS. For the genetic analysis, participants without genotyping data were excluded (see Supplementary material online, *Figure S1*).

### Exposure and outcomes (The primary exposure was chronological age. The primary outcomes were subclinical vascular measures: cIMT and PWV.

…

#### Lipid traitsreSerum total cholesterol and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol levels were measured using an automated enzymatic method. Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol was not included due to substantial missing data in the earlier RS cohorts (RS-I to RS-III), where it was not routinely measured. Although available in more recent cycles, these data were not yet accessible for the current analysis. Triglyceride levels were also unavailable or inconsistently measured, and could not be reliably estimated from total and HDL cholesterol alone due to the lack of fasting status and very LDL data.

### Covariates assessmente Information on study covariates, including health status, medical history, lifestyle, and medications, was collected at baseline using comprehensive computerized questionnaires conducted at participants’ homes by trained interviewers. These data were verified through extensive clinical and laboratory assessments at the research centre. Body mass index (BMI) in kg/m² was calculated by dividing weight by the square of height.

…

### Statistical analysis SBaseline characteristics were summarized using mean (SD) for continuous variables and proportions for categorical variables. Variables with less than 5% missing data were imputed using the R package [mice].^27^ The specific variables imputed included hsCRP (2.3% missing), BMI (0.9%), total cholesterol (1.4%), HDL (1.6%), systolic blood pressure (SBP) (0.8%), diastolic blood pressure (DBP) (0.8%), and pulse rate (1.5%).

…

For PWV, which was measured cross-sectionally, we used spline-based linear regression models (See Supplementary material online, Supplementary Methods for detailed methodology). To examine sex and age differences in age-related vascular dysfunction trajectories, we incorporated interaction terms in the models. A two-way interaction (sex × follow-up time) tested whether cIMT changes over time differed between males and females, while a three-way interaction (age × sex × follow-up time) assessed whether sex differences in cIMT trajectories varied by age group.

…

^29,30^ Supplementary material online, *Figure S2* illustrates the analysis flow, time points, and beta coefficients. We fitted a linear regression model (without spline terms) to examine the association between age (T~0~) and hsCRP (T~0~), adjusting for sex, BMI, prevalent CVD (yes/no), hypertension, and co-medications (blood pressure-lowering agents, glucose-lowering agents, cardiac medications, and lipid-lowering medications) to determine β~1~.
Another linear regression model was fitted to analyse the associations between total cholesterol (T~0~), HDL (T~0~), and age (T~0~), adjusting for the same set of variables to determine β~2~ and β~3~, respectively. The regression coefficients (β1, β2, β3) represent the effect of hsCRP and lipids on vascular outcomes while controlling for these confounders.
Finally, we performed a linear mixed model (without spline terms) to investigate the associations between age (β~0~), hsCRP (α~1~), total cholesterol (α~2~), HDL (α~3~), and longitudinal changes (multiple measurements) in cIMT (T~0~; T~1~) and cross-sectional PWV(T~0~).
We accounted for varying baseline levels among individuals by including a random intercept for each subject in the mixed model of the cIMT outcome. This model was adjusted for the confounders as mentioned above, as well as sub-cohort, IMT scan follow-up time, systolic/diastolic blood pressure, pulse rate, and hypertension. hsCRP was natural log transformed to hold the normal distribution assumption of linear regression. All these mediation analyses were accompanied by reported percentages of mediation relative to the total effect without use of the spline terms. These percentages reflect statistical mediation, but not necessarily causal pathways, particularly for cross-sectional outcomes.
We further examined the genetic evidence supporting a causal relationship between hsCRP and cIMT, as well as PWV, from a genetic predisposition perspective using publicly available genetic datasets. Genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary data were sourced from the CHARGE Consortium for hsCRP,^31^ the UK Biobank for PWV,^32^ and the AWI-Gen study for cIMT,^33^ which are the largest and most updated sources.
Detailed characteristics of these studies are presented in Supplementary material online, *Table S1*. We applied three complementary MR methods, inverse variance-weighted (IVW), weighted median, and MR-Egger, to account for pleiotropy and assess robustness. Harmonization procedures ensured consistent SNP alignment across datasets, and sensitivity analyses, including leave-one-out tests and Cochrane’s *Q*, were conducted. Results are reported as beta coefficients with 95% confidence intervals (see Supplementary material online, Supplementary Methods for detailed methodology).
Significant SNPs (*P* < 0.05) derived from both cIMT and PWV MR analysis (see Supplementary material online, *Table S2*) were used for further investigation and pathway analysis in RS. Details of the sex-stratified analyses, SNP replication in the RS, and pathway enrichment procedures are provided in the Supplementary material online, Supplementary Methods. All statistical analyses were performed using R v.4.3.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Austria).

## Resultssi### Baseline characteristicsorBaseline characteristics of participants included in the cIMT and PWV analyses are presented in *Table 1*, stratified by sex. The participants in the cIMT mediation analysis (*n* = 7591) had a mean (± SD) age of 61.6 years (±7.37), and 57.1% (*n* = 4337) were females.
The median follow-up period between the baseline (first measurement) and follow-up IMT (second measurement) was 6.54 years [2.86, 21.9]. Furthermore, participants included in the PWV mediation analysis had a mean age of 64.1 years (±7.56), with 55.7% (*n* = 3617) being female. Sex-based differences in cardiometabolic factors (e.g. blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, CVD history) were observed and adjusted for in all multivariable models.

### Mediation analysis chsCRP was evaluated as the potential mediator in the association between age and vascular dysfunction, as measured by cIMT progression and cross-sectional PWV. Significant mediation effects were observed for hsCRP in both outcomes after adjustment for relevant confounders, including hypertension. The 2.66% association between age and cIMT progression was mediated by hsCRP (Sobel *P* = 0.001, percent mediated = 2.66%, based on a mixed effect model).
